1. When that test was [introduced](https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/1935) it was the first, and only test of timeouts in the test suite. It seems to be named that way because it was added when the handling for timeouts on requests where the `stream` parameter is `True`, but the test isn't actually setting `stream=True`. The accompanying code change actually removed a branch in the timeout handling code - it used to only set connect timeouts when stream was true, but after the change, it set both connect and read timeouts regardless of the value of stream. So really, this test is just testing read timeouts.

1. The next thing to notice is that now there are a lot more tests around timeouts, and today we have [test_read_timeout](https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/main/tests/test_requests.py#L2568-L2576) which runs the other 2 tests that use the `delay/10` httbin endpoint that's causing the slow tests. I'm pretty sure that's effectively testing the same thing as `test_stream_timeout`. The `test_read_timeout` calls both set the connect timeout to None and only test read timeouts, where the `test_stream_timeout` call is using a scalar so both connect and read timeouts are set to the same value, but the test is written to succeed when it returns an exception with "Read timed out" in the args.

1. The final nail in the coffin for test_stream_timeout is that the way that test is written, it will actually pass the test (false positive) if the request succeeds without timing out. If you look at how all of the other timeout tests are written, there's a `pytest.fail()` after the get request that's supposed to time out - so if the exception doesn't get raised, the test fails. That's not there on `test_stream_timeout`, so if the exception doesn't happen, the test completes and doesn't record a failure.

1. The only case that I can see where `test_stream_timeout` is doing anything that's not currently covered by one of the other tests is testing that using a simple scalar type for the timeout parameter is accepted. We can add that test to `test_total_timeout_connect` which doesn't use httpbin.

It also looks like httbin `delay` allows floating point values, not just integers. Initially, these tests were all configured to run across the internet to `httpbin.org` so I think the `delay/10` that was originally chosen made sense because the internet connection might be slow or flaky during tests and allowing for a longer test window might have made the tests more reliable, but as the tests now run locally, that should be less of a concern. The 10 second delay also was being borne by the server and didn't have any impact on the test suite's execution speed - which was only bound by the local timeout. I feel like we could probably reliably switch it to `delay/0.25` so the httbin server would only block for 250ms twice. That seems like it should be long enough to reliably run a test that should time out in 100ms - but we could even drop the timeout parameter to 0.05 - and make it a 50msec timeout against an endpoint that lasts 250ms for a bit more buffer.

While we're at it, we can DRY up the repeated `0.1` parameter everywhere and make all of the timeouts consistently faster.

`proxy_bypass_registry()` in `src/requests/utils.py` builds a pattern from the Windows `ProxyOverride` registry value and matches it with `re.match()`, which **only anchors the start**. An override for `google.com` therefore also matched `google.com.evil.com`:

```python
test = test.replace(".", r"\.")   # mask dots
test = test.replace("*", r".*")   # change glob sequence
test = test.replace("?", r".")    # change glob char
if re.match(test, host, re.I):    # start-anchored only
    return True
```

Consequence: an attacker-influenced hostname can escape a proxy that was configured to inspect its traffic.

### Fix

Append `\Z` so the override must match the entire host:

```python
if re.match(test + r"\Z", host, re.I):
    return True
```

The glob translation is untouched, so existing overrides (`*.example.net`, `?`, etc.) keep behaving exactly as before — only unanchored suffix matches are now rejected.

Note: this function descends from an old copy of CPython's `proxy_bypass`, which now matches with `fnmatch` (anchored at both ends, wildcards preserved). Anchoring here is the **minimal** fix with no change to glob semantics; switching to `fnmatch` would also resolve the issue and better tracks CPython, if maintainers prefer that direction.

### Verification

Reproduced locally on Windows (Python 3.13, requests main @ `448d64a`-era):

- Before fix: `proxy_bypass_registry("google.com.evil.com")` → `True` (the bypass)
- After fix: `False`, while `google.com` → `True` and `*.example.net` still matches `a.example.net` → `True`
- Full `tests/test_utils.py`: 229 passed, 1 skipped

This repository limits pull request creation to collaborators, so the branch is available on my fork instead:

- Branch: `https://github.com/Xx-173/requests/tree/fix/proxy-bypass-anchored-match`
- Commit: `3984164e`

It contains the one-line fix above plus `test_proxy_bypass_registry_does_not_match_host_suffixes` in `tests/test_utils.py` (Windows-only, matching the existing registry tests), which asserts:

- `proxy_bypass_registry("google.com")` is `True` (exact override still works)
- `proxy_bypass_registry("a.example.net")` is `True` (`*.example.net` glob still works)
- `proxy_bypass_registry("google.com.evil.com")` is `False` (suffix escape blocked)
- `proxy_bypass_registry("notgoogle.com")` is `False`

## The change

`src/requests/utils.py`:

```diff
             test = test.replace(".", r"\.")  # mask dots
             test = test.replace("*", r".*")  # change glob sequence
             test = test.replace("?", r".")  # change glob char
-            if re.match(test, host, re.I):
+            # The whole host must match. re.match only anchors the start, so
+            # "example.com" would also bypass the proxy for "example.com.evil.net".
+            if re.fullmatch(test, host, re.I):
                 return True
         return False
```

`re.fullmatch` is the smallest change that makes the intent explicit, and it matches what the `no_proxy` path already does — `test_should_bypass_proxies` in `tests/test_utils.py` already covers "does not greedily match domains that merely endswith the no_proxy entry. The `<local>` branch above returns before reaching the pattern match, so it is unaffected.

| URL | ProxyOverride | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `http://example.com.evil.net/` | `example.com` | `False` (was `True`) |
| `http://notexample.com/` | `example.com` | `False` (control, unchanged) |
| `http://www.example.com/` | `*.example.com` | `True` (control: globs still work) |
| `http://www.example.com.evil.net/` | `*.example.com` | `False` (was `True`) |

- Before: `2 failed, 14 passed`.
- After: `16 passed`.
- `pytest tests/test_utils.py` → 232 passed, 1 skipped.
- `ruff check` clean on both files.

The new cases inherit the existing `skipif(os.name != "nt")` guard, since `proxy_bypass_registry` only exists on `win32`.

This still reproduces on 2.32.4:

```python

UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode characters in position 4-6: surrogates not allowed
```

It comes from '_encode_params' in 'models.p',, where each value is encoded with 'v.encode("utf-8")'.

I don't think requests can reasonably make this call succeed -- unpaired surrogates genuinely can't be represented in UTF-8, and re-encoding with 'errors="surrogateescape"' would silently put mangled bytes on the wire and hide what is usually a decoding bug in the caller's own code. What does seem worth improving is the error itself: right now it reports a byte offset into an intermediate value and gives no hint which field caused it, which is awkward on a request with many fields.

I have a change that keeps the behaviour identical but makes the message name the offending field:
```
UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode characters in position 4-6:
surrogates not allowed; the value for field 'name' contains an unpaired UTF-16 surrogate that cannot be represented in UTF-8 -- check that the input was decoded correctly before passing it to requests
```

It re-raises the same **UnicodeEncodeError** type rather than introducing a new exception, so anything already catching **UnicodeEncodeError** around a request keeps working. Two files, +49/-2, with a regression test; 'ruff format' and 'ruff check' are clean and the existing tests pass.

import requests
